z-m-04-01.title: What could the next card drawn be?
z-m-04-01.topic: Possibility: saying what can come up and what cannot
z-m-04-01.goal: Each time a card is taken out, fix and state 'it can come up / it cannot come up / it must come up' with a reason.
z-m-04-01.material: In a box there are 6 number cards, with 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 written on them, one on each. The backs of the cards are all the same, so you draw one at a time with your eyes closed. After you check the front of a drawn card, you put it to the side and do not put it back in the box. The notices below open one at a time.
z-m-04-01.thinking.0: Fixing a judgment with newly learned information
z-m-04-01.thinking.1: Telling 'it might come up' and 'it must come up' apart
z-m-04-01.thinking.2: Doubting plausible-sounding reasons like size or order
z-m-04-01.prereq.0: Knowing the numbers from 1 to 10 and telling odd and even apart (Grade 1 level)
z-m-04-01.prereq.1: Telling 'there is' and 'there is not' apart when you say it
z-m-04-01.s.s1.prompt: The notices open one at a time. Each time, choose the right statement.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each notice, first write 'which cards are left in the box now'.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the statement you chose is really right by working out, for each remaining card, whether it can come up.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.0.info: No card has been drawn yet. Think about the first card you will draw.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.0.after: Every card in the box can come up, and a card that is not in the box, like 7, cannot come up. You cannot decide ahead of time which card will come up.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You saw that there is a 5 in the box, so it can come up. It is a good idea to look at the cards that are there first.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: In the box there are only cards 1 to 6. Look again at whether a card that is not in the box can come up.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: If you draw with your eyes closed, you cannot decide ahead of time which card it will be. 'Might come up' and 'must come up' are different.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: The card that comes up is one of 1 to 6
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You went over all the cards in the box and said the range of what can come up. You did not decide which number.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.1.info: You drew two cards and got 5 and 2. You put the two cards to the side and did not put them back in the box. Now think about the third card you will draw.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.1.after: 5 and 2 left the box and do not go back in. So 5 can no longer come up, and the remaining cards 1, 3, 4, and 6 can all come up. The new information changed one of the first ideas.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 5 might come up again, like at first
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You thought of the situation as it was at first. Look at where the 5 is now.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 5 and 2 came up, so this time it's 1's turn in order
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: There is no fixed 'turn'. If you draw with your eyes closed, every remaining card can come up.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: One of the remaining cards 1, 3, 4, 6 comes up
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You looked only at the cards left in the box, leaving out the cards put to the side. You used the new information in your judgment.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: 5 and 2 already came up, so this time 6 must come up
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Because some cards have already come up, the next card is not decided. Look at how many cards are left.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.2.info: 4 came up as the third card. You put the 4 to the side too. Now three cards, 1, 3, and 6, are left in the box.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: Choose the right statement about the fourth card you will draw.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.2.after: Among the remaining cards 1, 3, 6, there are odd (1, 3) and even (6). So both can come up. Even though there are fewer cards, it is still true that you cannot decide ahead of time which card will come up.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: An even card cannot come up
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Check one by one whether there is an even number among the remaining cards.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 6 is the biggest number, so 6 is the most likely to come up
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: A bigger number is not drawn more easily. The backs of the cards are all the same and you draw with your eyes closed.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The 4 was put to the side. Check whether 4 is in the box now.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: An odd card and an even card can both come up
z-m-04-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You looked at the fact that there are both odd and even numbers among the remaining 1, 3, 6.
z-m-04-01.s.s1.reflect: How did your idea that 5 might come up change after the 5 was put to the side? And which statement stayed the same even after more cards were drawn?
z-m-04-01.s.s2.prompt: A friend said, "The cards left are 1, 3, and 6, so the biggest, 6, will come up!" What would you like to say to this friend?
z-m-04-01.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether it is okay to change "will come up" in your friend's words to "might come up".
z-m-04-01.s.s2.hint.1: Work out whether it is really impossible for a card other than 6 to come up among the three remaining cards.
z-m-04-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does the difference between 'might come up' and 'must come up' show in what I said?
z-m-04-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you think about the fact that other cards among the remaining 1, 3, 6 can come up too?
z-m-04-01.s.s2.model.0: 6 might come up, but it does not have to. 1 or 3 might come up.
z-m-04-01.s.s2.modelNote.0: It looked at all the cards that can come up.
z-m-04-01.s.s2.model.1: A bigger number does not come up more easily. You draw with your eyes closed, so you cannot know which card will come up.
z-m-04-01.s.s2.model.2: A 6 could come out, but not necessarily. A 1 or a 3 could come out too.

z-m-04-02.title: When I count, the two friends' numbers are different
z-m-04-02.topic: Counting without missing any: finding where the counting went wrong
z-m-04-02.goal: When two people's counts are different, use the number in each row as evidence, learn that neither may be right, and find the mistake and say a counting method that prevents the same mistake.
z-m-04-02.material: On a desk there are identical star stickers in three rows. The top row has 5, the middle row has 6, and the bottom row has 5. Jihu and Nari counted how many stickers there are in all. Jihu said 15, and Nari said 17. You want to find out which of the two friends is right.
z-m-04-02.thinking.0: Checking with evidence (the number in each row) when the results are different
z-m-04-02.thinking.1: Finding the wrong row in the counting
z-m-04-02.thinking.2: Thinking of ways to prevent missing and double counting
z-m-04-02.prereq.0: Counting numbers up to 20 in order (Grade 1 level)
z-m-04-02.prereq.1: Counting each row separately and writing it down
z-m-04-02.s.s1.prompt: Look at the numbers the two friends counted and choose the right statement.
z-m-04-02.s.s1.hint.0: First write how many there are in each row.
z-m-04-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the total from counting all three rows is the same as the numbers the two friends counted.
z-m-04-02.s.s1.r.a: A smaller number is not necessarily right. Check what happens when you put together the numbers in each row.
z-m-04-02.s.s1.r.b: You checked both numbers using the number in each row.
z-m-04-02.s.s1.r.c: You thought the one who counted more did not miss any. But you can also count the same sticker twice.
z-m-04-02.s.s1.o.d: We cannot tell who is right
z-m-04-02.s.s1.r.d: The number in each row is already known. Look again at whether you can check with that.
z-m-04-02.s.s1.explain: If you count the top row 5, the middle row 6, and the bottom row 5, there are 16. Neither the 15 Jihu counted nor the 17 Nari counted is right. Both friends made a mistake somewhere while counting.
z-m-04-02.s.s2.prompt: This is how Jihu counted aloud. Choose the wrong row.
z-m-04-02.s.s2.hint.0: Count how many were counted in each row and compare it with the known number.
z-m-04-02.s.s2.hint.1: In the words used to count the bottom row, point with a finger to see how many were counted.
z-m-04-02.s.s2.line.0: He counted the top row from the left: one, two, three, four, five.
z-m-04-02.s.s2.line.1: He counted the middle row from the left, continuing: six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven.
z-m-04-02.s.s2.line.2: He counted the bottom row from the left, continuing: twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen.
z-m-04-02.s.s2.line.3: The last number counted is fifteen, so there are 15 in all.
z-m-04-02.s.s2.explain: Row 3 is wrong. The bottom row has 5 stickers, but he counted only 4: twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen. Sixteen was missed. Rows 1 and 2 were counted to match the number in each row, and row 4 just repeated the last number counted before, so it is not a mistake in the way of counting itself.
z-m-04-02.s.s3.prompt: Nari said 17. Guess where Nari might have gone wrong, and write a counting method that can prevent the same mistake.
z-m-04-02.s.s3.hint.0: First look at whether 17 is more or less than 16, and think about whether something was missed or counted extra.
z-m-04-02.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what kind of mark on the ones you counted would keep you from counting the same sticker twice.
z-m-04-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the mistake I guessed fit the number 17?
z-m-04-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: If I use the method I wrote, can it prevent both Jihu's mistake and Nari's mistake?
z-m-04-02.s.s3.model.0: It seems the same star was counted twice. If you count while making a small mark on the stars you counted, you will not count twice or miss any.
z-m-04-02.s.s3.model.1: It seems one was counted one more time between the middle row and the bottom row. If you count each row separately and write it down, then link them later, you can find the wrong row.
z-m-04-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: Counting each row and writing it down

z-m-04-03.title: A stain hides one box
z-m-04-03.topic: Hidden data in a table: what more do we need to find it?
z-m-04-03.goal: Choose the information needed to find out one box of a table (the total number, whether each person chose only one thing), and say how the answer changes when new information arrives.
z-m-04-03.material: The friends in our class each chose one kind of vehicle they like. Paint got on one box of the survey table, so it cannot be seen. [Table] Car 6 / Train □ (cannot be seen) / Airplane 4 / Ship 2. You want to know the number that goes in the empty box (□).
z-m-04-03.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-04-03.thinking.2: Fixing your judgment by putting in new information
z-m-04-03.prereq.0: Adding and subtracting numbers up to 20 (Grade 1 level)
z-m-04-03.prereq.1: Reading the number of people in each box of the table
z-m-04-03.s.s1.prompt: What more do you need to know to find the number that goes in □? Choose all the right ones.
z-m-04-03.s.s1.hint.0: First check all the numbers in the boxes that are known in the table.
z-m-04-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how that number must relate to the whole class.
z-m-04-03.s.s1.o.a: Which group the 4 who chose airplane are in
z-m-04-03.s.s1.r.a: Who is in which group has nothing to do with the number in □. Look again at the information you need to decide the number.
z-m-04-03.s.s1.o.b: Whether the friends who chose train are on the tall side
z-m-04-03.s.s1.r.b: Height has nothing to do with the number in □. Think about what information would let you decide the number.
z-m-04-03.s.s1.o.c: How many friends there are in all in the class
z-m-04-03.s.s1.r.c: You tried to match the total of the table with the known boxes.
z-m-04-03.s.s1.o.e: Whether each person chose only one thing
z-m-04-03.s.s1.r.e: You tried to check that nobody appears in two boxes.
z-m-04-03.s.s2.prompt: The teacher told you. "There are 15 of us in our class. One friend was absent today, so we could not survey that friend. Every friend who was surveyed chose only one thing." How many is □?
z-m-04-03.s.s2.hint.0: The absent friend does not appear anywhere in the table. First decide how many people must appear in the table.
z-m-04-03.s.s2.hint.1: Compare that number with the numbers in the three known boxes.
z-m-04-03.s.s2.r.a: It looks like you used the whole class of 15 as it is. Check the information that there is a friend who was not surveyed.
z-m-04-03.s.s2.r.b: Now you know the total number of people and that each chose only one thing. Check again whether that information lets you decide □.
z-m-04-03.s.s2.r.c: You matched the known boxes against the number of people surveyed. You used the information that a friend was absent.
z-m-04-03.s.s2.r.d: Check what you left out while counting the numbers in the known boxes.
z-m-04-03.s.s2.explain: The friends who were surveyed are 14, which is 15 minus the 1 absent. The known boxes are 6 + 4 + 2 = 12, so □ is 14 − 12 = 2.
z-m-04-03.s.s3.prompt: If one more friend had been absent, how many friends would have chosen train? Write how you knew.
z-m-04-03.s.s3.hint.0: Read again how many the total was that you used just now to find □.
z-m-04-03.s.s3.hint.1: First say what happens to that total if one more friend is absent.
z-m-04-03.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If more friends are absent, ...
z-m-04-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did the numbers I wrote use both the numbers in the three known boxes and the number of people surveyed?
z-m-04-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why only □ changes, and not the other boxes, when one more friend is absent?
z-m-04-03.s.s3.model.0: 1. The friends surveyed drop by one to 13, so after putting together the known 6, 4, and 2, what is left is 1.
z-m-04-03.s.s3.modelNote.0: Explained by the 13 minus the 12 counted in all the known boxes, the number left
z-m-04-03.s.s3.model.1: One. The total went down by one but the other boxes stay the same, so the train box goes down by one.
z-m-04-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: Explained by the change in the total
z-m-04-03.s.s1.o.d: Whether the numbers in the three known cells (car, airplane, ship) are right
z-m-04-03.s.s1.r.d: The numbers in the known cells are already in the table. To decide □, you need information that is not in the table.
z-m-04-03.s.s1.explain: If you know the total number of people in the class and that each person chose only one thing, the number left after subtracting the three known cells is □. Knowing the height or name of a friend who chose the train, or just rechecking the known cells, cannot decide □.
z-m-04-03.s.s3.model.2: 1 person. The number of people surveyed becomes 13 and the known cells are 12, so 13-12=1.

z-m-04-04.title: Does the 'most' always beat all the rest?
z-m-04-04.topic: Making a counterexample: comparing the most-chosen thing with all the rest together
z-m-04-04.goal: Make a table in which the claim 'the activity chosen most always has more than all the others put together' does not hold, and say the condition under which the claim becomes right.
z-m-04-04.material: 12 friends chose the activity they want to do on a picnic. The activities are treasure hunt, jump rope, and ball games. All 12 chose just one thing. Hayun said, "The activity chosen most always has more than the friends who chose the other two activities put together!" Assume there is only one activity chosen most, and it is not tied with another activity.
z-m-04-04.thinking.0: Making a counterexample to the claim 'always'
z-m-04-04.thinking.2: Finding the condition under which the claim is right
z-m-04-04.prereq.1: Finding the biggest item in a table
z-m-04-04.s.s1.prompt: Is Hayun's claim always right? Before making a table, choose your thought.
z-m-04-04.s.s1.hint.0: Put in one small number and write one case.
z-m-04-04.s.s1.hint.1: Put side by side the number for the most-chosen activity and the number you get by adding the other two activities.
z-m-04-04.s.s1.o.a: It is always right. The most-chosen activity has more than the other activities
z-m-04-04.s.s1.r.a: 'More than each of the other activities' and 'more than all the rest put together' do not mean the same thing.
z-m-04-04.s.s1.o.b: It does not seem to be always right. I will test it by putting in numbers
z-m-04-04.s.s1.r.b: You saw that the claim says 'always', so it is worth testing. It is an attitude of checking with numbers.
z-m-04-04.s.s1.o.c: I don't know. We can't tell because it's 12 people
z-m-04-04.s.s1.r.c: The number of people is fixed. Think about whether you can find out by putting in a number.
z-m-04-04.s.s1.explain: The word 'always' can be broken by even one example. You can find out by testing with a table you make yourself. A student who said 'I don't know' at first can also judge after making a table.
z-m-04-04.s.s1.acc.0: At first you may not know. You can find out by making a table and testing. It's fine if you want to test it.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 tables in which Hayun's claim is not right. Write the number of friends for the most-chosen activity as a, the second as b, and the third as c. (a, b, and c are natural numbers that are 0 or more, and all three add up to 12 friends.)
z-m-04-04.s.s2.hint.0: First choose a number a of friends for the most-chosen activity.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.hint.1: Count the friends who chose the other two activities together and compare with a.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.hint.2: There must not be a tie. Check that a is greater than b and c.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.var.a: Number of friends for the most-chosen activity (a)
z-m-04-04.s.s2.var.b: Number of friends for another activity (b)
z-m-04-04.s.s2.var.c: Number of friends for the remaining activity (c)
z-m-04-04.s.s2.ok.c1: The number of friends is a natural number that is 0 or more.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of friends must be a natural number that is 0 or more.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.ok.c2: All 12 friends chose one thing each.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.fail.c2: All three numbers must add up to 12 friends.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.ok.c3: a is the most-chosen activity (there is no tie).
z-m-04-04.s.s2.fail.c3: a must be greater than both b and c.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.ok.c4: The most-chosen activity does not have more than the rest put together, so Hayun's claim breaks.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.fail.c4: In this table, the most-chosen activity has more than the rest put together, so Hayun's claim does not break.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.explain: With 5, 4, 3, the 5 who chose most are fewer than the rest, 4 + 3 = 7. With 6, 3, 3, the 6 is equal to the rest, 3 + 3 = 6, so you cannot say 'more'. So Hayun's claim is not always right. One table is enough.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.because.prompt: Pick one of the tables you made and write how you would show a friend that Hayun's claim is wrong.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: Pick one table and first write the number for the most-chosen activity.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare that number with the number you get by counting the friends who chose the other two activities together.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: In the table I picked, did you say with numbers why the most-chosen activity does not have more than the other two put together?
z-m-04-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you know and write that one table is enough to break the word 'always'?
z-m-04-04.s.s2.because.model.0: If it is treasure hunt 5, jump rope 4, ball games 3, treasure hunt is the most, but it is fewer than the 7 for jump rope and ball games put together.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.because.model.1: If it is 6, 3, 3, the 6 who chose most are equal to the 6 you get by putting together the other 3 and 3, so you cannot say it is more.
z-m-04-04.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: Used the equal case as the counterexample
z-m-04-04.s.s3.prompt: For Hayun's claim to always be right, what would have to be different? Choose all the right ones.
z-m-04-04.s.s3.hint.0: Compare with the tables you made so far, and think about what would have to be different for Hayun's claim not to break.
z-m-04-04.s.s3.hint.1: Change the number for the most-chosen activity one at a time and compare it with the sum of the rest.
z-m-04-04.s.s3.o.a: When the friends increased from 12 to 15
z-m-04-04.s.s3.r.a: Even if there are more people, you can make similar tables. What does a table tested with 15 look like?
z-m-04-04.s.s3.o.b: When there are only two activities and the number of friends is different
z-m-04-04.s.s3.r.b: You looked at the fact that when there are only two activities, the most-chosen one is compared with the rest (the one other activity).
z-m-04-04.s.s3.o.c: When a friend can choose two activities
z-m-04-04.s.s3.r.c: If one person is counted twice, only the total number changes, and the problem of comparing stays the same.
z-m-04-04.s.s3.o.d: When the most-chosen activity has 7 or more
z-m-04-04.s.s3.r.d: You worked out that if 7 or more of the 12 chose the same activity, the rest is 5 or fewer.
z-m-04-04.s.s3.explain: If there are only two activities and the numbers of friends are different, the one chosen by more has more than the rest (the one other activity). With three activities and 12 friends, when the most-chosen activity has 7 or more, the rest is 5 or fewer, so the most-chosen one has more. Even if you increase to 15, there are tables that break it, like 6, 5, 4.

z-m-04-05.title: A survey of favorite colors: which boxes do we need?
z-m-04-05.topic: Deciding the survey items: making boxes that everyone can mark without leaving anyone out
z-m-04-05.goal: Learn the problem that arises when a survey box is missing an item, make boxes yourself so that every friend can mark one box, and say the limit of the new box that appears.
z-m-04-05.material: The 20 students in Minho's class are doing a survey of 'one favorite color'. Each person marks only one box. Minho made only three boxes on the survey form: 'red', 'blue', and 'yellow'.
z-m-04-05.thinking.0: Finding what is missing in the survey boxes
z-m-04-05.thinking.1: Designing an alternative (many ways are possible)
z-m-04-05.thinking.2: Interpreting the result of the 'other' box
z-m-04-05.prereq.0: Marking and counting in boxes divided in a table (Grade 1 level)
z-m-04-05.prereq.1: Understanding the condition that each person picks only one thing
z-m-04-05.s.s1.prompt: If the 20 people mark only these three boxes, what could happen?
z-m-04-05.s.s1.hint.0: Think of a few colors that friends might like.
z-m-04-05.s.s1.hint.1: Check one by one whether each color is among the three boxes.
z-m-04-05.s.s1.o.a: If you count all the marks in the three boxes, it must be 20
z-m-04-05.s.s1.r.a: There may be friends who have no box to mark. First work out whether every friend can pick a box.
z-m-04-05.s.s1.r.d: You are guessing the result of the boxes ahead of time. Right now, the first thing is whether every friend can mark.
z-m-04-05.s.s1.explain: If there are only three boxes, a friend whose favorite color is not one of the three, like green or purple, has no box to mark. Then even if you count all the marks, it may not come to 20.
z-m-04-05.s.s2.prompt: How should you make the boxes so that all 20 people can mark their favorite color? Write the box names, and also write why you made them that way.
z-m-04-05.s.s2.hint.0: If there is a friend among the 20 whose favorite color is not red, blue, or yellow, think about which box they will mark.
z-m-04-05.s.s2.hint.1: If you make one more box, write what name it would need so that everyone can mark.
z-m-04-05.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Besides the red, blue, and yellow boxes, I make a ... box. Because ...
z-m-04-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: In the boxes I made, can all 20 people mark one box?
z-m-04-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is there any case where one person has to mark two boxes?
z-m-04-05.s.s2.model.0: I will make boxes for red, blue, yellow, green, and other colors. If there is an 'other colors' box, anyone can mark no matter which color they like.
z-m-04-05.s.s2.model.1: First ask the friends their favorite colors, and make a box for each color that comes up. Then there is no friend who cannot choose because there is no box.
z-m-04-05.s.s2.modelNote.1: Ask first, then decide the boxes
z-m-04-05.s.s3.prompt: Minho fixed the boxes to 'red, blue, yellow, green, other colors' and surveyed the 20 people. The result is red 4, blue 4, yellow 3, green 3, and other colors 6. Jisu said, "Other colors has 6, the most, so other colors is the most popular color." How should Jisu's statement be fixed?
z-m-04-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write a few colors that could fit in the other-colors box.
z-m-04-05.s.s3.hint.1: Think about the case where all 6 chose the same color and the case where all 6 chose different colors.
z-m-04-05.s.s3.o.a: That's right. 6 is the biggest number, so other colors is the most popular color
z-m-04-05.s.s3.r.a: You compared only the numbers in the boxes. First think about whether 'other colors' is one color.
z-m-04-05.s.s3.o.b: Erase the other-colors box and say red and blue are the most popular
z-m-04-05.s.s3.r.b: Even if you remove a box, the 6 who chose other colors do not disappear. You cannot know which colors those 6 chose.
z-m-04-05.s.s3.explain: 'Other colors' may contain several colors together, like purple and pink. If the 6 each chose a different color, one color may have only 1 person, and if all 6 chose the same color, one color may have 6 people. This table alone cannot tell which it is, so you need to ask those 6 once more which color it is.
z-m-04-05.s.s1.o.b: A friend whose favorite color is green has no cell to mark
z-m-04-05.s.s1.r.b: I matched the colors the friends like to the cells of the survey table one by one.
z-m-04-05.s.s1.o.c: There are only three cells, so the survey cannot be done at all
z-m-04-05.s.s1.r.c: Having few cells does not mean the survey cannot be done. Look at when the cells really become a problem.
z-m-04-05.s.s1.o.d: Red will get the most marks, so the other cells are not needed
z-m-04-05.s.s3.o.c: There are five cells, so this result cannot be trusted
z-m-04-05.s.s3.r.c: Having few or many cells does not mean the result cannot be trusted. Look at what information the cells give.
z-m-04-05.s.s3.o.d: "Other colors" is a cell where many colors are mixed, so it cannot be called one color
z-m-04-05.s.s3.r.d: You noticed that many colors are gathered in one cell. You looked at the point that we cannot tell whether all 6 people in the cell have the same color.

z-m-04-06.title: To say how many more there are
z-m-04-06.topic: Comparing the counts of two sets of data: comparing by pairing and counting separately
z-m-04-06.goal: Compare two ways of finding out 'how many more', by pairing and by the numbers counted separately, and make different survey results that have the same difference.
z-m-04-06.material: The friends in the class each chose one favorite animal, a puppy or a cat. A friend who chose a puppy is shown with ○ (circle), and a friend who chose a cat is shown with △ (triangle). 8 friends chose a puppy and 5 friends chose a cat. Seohyeon put a row of ○ and a row of △ side by side, one above the other.
z-m-04-06.thinking.1: Making many tables with the same difference
z-m-04-06.thinking.2: Explaining why the difference does not change
z-m-04-06.prereq.0: Comparing sizes of numbers up to 20 and subtracting (Grade 1 level)
z-m-04-06.prereq.1: Comparing by pairing one by one
z-m-04-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the right ways to find out how many more friends chose a puppy than chose a cat.
z-m-04-06.s.s1.hint.0: Put 8 ○ and 5 △ one above the other and connect them one by one.
z-m-04-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the numbers you get from the ways you chose are the same.
z-m-04-06.s.s1.o.a: Pair the ○ and △ one by one and count the ○ that have no partner
z-m-04-06.s.s1.r.a: You matched the two rows one by one and looked at the leftovers for the difference. It is the way of comparing by pairing.
z-m-04-06.s.s1.o.b: Count together all the friends who chose a puppy and a cat
z-m-04-06.s.s1.r.b: The number counted altogether is the total number of friends surveyed. Work out whether it is a number that tells 'how many more'.
z-m-04-06.s.s1.o.c: Count back from 8 to 5 and count how many steps you pass
z-m-04-06.s.s1.r.c: You found the difference by counting between the two numbers. It is a different path from pairing, but a way of finding the same difference.
z-m-04-06.s.s1.o.d: Just say 8, the bigger of 8 and 5
z-m-04-06.s.s1.r.d: The bigger number is the number of friends who chose a puppy. You have not yet said how many more there are.
z-m-04-06.s.s1.explain: If you pair them up, 3 ○ are left over. Counting back from 8 to 5 is also 3 steps. The answers of the two ways are the same, 3 friends. The total counted, 13, or the bigger number, 8, is not 'how many more'.
z-m-04-06.s.s2.prompt: They did another survey on another day. Make 3 survey results in which exactly 3 more friends chose a puppy than chose a cat, and the friends who chose the two animals put together are 15 or fewer. (At least 1 friend chose a cat.)
z-m-04-06.s.s2.hint.0: First choose a number y of friends who chose a cat.
z-m-04-06.s.s2.hint.1: Choose x so that, when paired with the y you chose, 3 ○ are left over.
z-m-04-06.s.s2.hint.2: Check that the two numbers put together are 15 friends or fewer.
z-m-04-06.s.s2.var.x: Number of friends who chose a puppy (x)
z-m-04-06.s.s2.var.y: Number of friends who chose a cat (y)
z-m-04-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers of friends are natural numbers and at least 1 friend chose a cat.
z-m-04-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of friends must be natural numbers, and at least 1 friend must have chosen a cat.
z-m-04-06.s.s2.ok.c2: There are 3 more friends for puppy than for cat.
z-m-04-06.s.s2.fail.c2: Exactly 3 more friends must have chosen a puppy than a cat.
z-m-04-06.s.s2.ok.c3: Even put together, the two are 15 friends or fewer.
z-m-04-06.s.s2.fail.c3: The friends who chose the two animals must add up to 15 or fewer.
z-m-04-06.s.s2.explain: If 1 friend chose a cat, then puppy is 4; if 5, then 8; if 6, then 9. In every case, if you pair ○ and △, 3 ○ are left over. The sum must be 15 or fewer, so the number of friends who chose a cat can be up to 6.
z-m-04-06.s.s2.because.prompt: Even if the numbers of friends who chose a puppy and a cat are different in each table, it stays true that 'there are 3 more for puppy than for cat'. Write the reason in words that use pairing ○ and △.
z-m-04-06.s.s2.because.hint.0: Make a table where one more friend chose a cat, put it side by side with the first table, and pair ○ and △.
z-m-04-06.s.s2.because.hint.1: After pairing, count the ○ with no partner in each of the two tables and compare.
z-m-04-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you say how many ○ are left over after pairing?
z-m-04-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why the number of leftover ○ stays the same even when more friends choose a cat?
z-m-04-06.s.s2.because.model.0: If you pair ○ and △ one by one, in any table 3 ○ with no partner are left over. Even if both grow by the same amount, what is left stays 3.
z-m-04-06.s.s2.because.modelNote.0: The number left after pairing stays the same
z-m-04-06.s.s2.because.model.1: If one more friend chooses a cat, one more friend also chooses a puppy, so after pairing, the ○ left over is still 3.

z-m-04-07.title: There were many sunny days this week, so will next week be like that too?
z-m-04-07.topic: What the records can tell and cannot tell: guessing what will happen next
z-m-04-07.goal: Learn that from past records you can say what was 'the most', but you cannot state for sure what happens next, and say how your guess changes if you have more records.
z-m-04-07.material: You recorded the weather on the classroom calendar for 5 days, Monday to Friday. This week there were 3 sunny days, 1 cloudy day, and 1 rainy day. Yeonseo said, "There were the most sunny days this week, so next week there will be the most sunny days too."
z-m-04-07.thinking.0: Telling apart what the records can say and cannot say
z-m-04-07.thinking.1: Adjusting how sure you are as the data grows
z-m-04-07.thinking.2: Doubting statements that state things for sure
z-m-04-07.prereq.0: Adding numbers up to 5 and reading the number of days from a table (Grade 1 level)
z-m-04-07.prereq.1: Weather words like sunny, cloudy, rainy
z-m-04-07.s.s1.prompt: What do you think about Yeonseo's statement right now?
z-m-04-07.s.s1.hint.0: Compare whether the fact that sunny days were the most in this week's record and next week's weather are the same statement.
z-m-04-07.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine how it would be different if there were weather records for other weeks.
z-m-04-07.s.s1.explain: This week's record is a clue that there might be many sunny days next week. But with only one week's record, you cannot say 'definitely' that it will be so.
z-m-04-07.s.s1.acc.0: You saw well that one week's record cannot decide next week. But whether the record works as a clue can be worked out while collecting more.
z-m-04-07.s.s2.prompt: Yeonseo also found last week's record. Last week was 2 sunny days, 1 cloudy day, and 2 rainy days. Putting the two weeks (10 days) together, there are 5 sunny days, 2 cloudy days, and 3 rainy days. Choose the right statement.
z-m-04-07.s.s2.hint.0: Count the days of the two weeks again by weather and write them in a table.
z-m-04-07.s.s2.hint.1: Write separately what you can say from the records and what you do not know about next week.
z-m-04-07.s.s2.o.a: Sunny days were the most, so next week there will certainly be the most sunny days too
z-m-04-07.s.s2.r.a: Even if you collected ten days of records, next week has not come yet. The more you collect, the more clues you have, but you cannot state it for sure.
z-m-04-07.s.s2.explain: In the ten-day record, you can say that sunny days were the most, with 5 days. But next week's weather has not happened yet, so it cannot be decided. As the records grow, the clue that there might be many sunny days becomes a little more believable.
z-m-04-07.s.s3.hint.0: Look at whether the weeks with the most sunny days were the same in this week's and last week's records.
z-m-04-07.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what more you could learn if you collected the same kind of record for a few more weeks.
z-m-04-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In what I said, are 'what we can know from the current data' and 'what we do not know yet' separated?
z-m-04-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Would the records I said to collect more of help in guessing next week's weather?
z-m-04-07.s.s3.model.0: Sunny days might be the most, but not necessarily. If we collect the records of more weeks, we can trust it more.
z-m-04-07.s.s3.model.1: We can't know yet. Only two weeks is not enough, so we need to collect records of other weeks too and see how many times sunny days were the most.
z-m-04-07.s.s1.o.a: It might be, but we cannot say for sure
z-m-04-07.s.s1.r.a: You used past records as a clue but did not jump to a conclusion. You can think about how things might change if there were more records.
z-m-04-07.s.s1.o.b: This week's records tell us nothing about next week
z-m-04-07.s.s1.r.b: This week's records do not decide next week, but it is a pity to say there is no clue at all. A clue and certainty are different things.
z-m-04-07.s.s1.o.c: It was like that this week, so next week it will definitely be like that too
z-m-04-07.s.s1.r.c: You carried one week's records straight over to next week. Other weeks might have been different.
z-m-04-07.s.s2.o.b: Sunny days were the most, but we cannot know about next week
z-m-04-07.s.s2.r.b: You separated what the records can tell us (it was the most) from what they cannot (next week).
z-m-04-07.s.s2.o.c: There were more rainy days than sunny days
z-m-04-07.s.s2.r.c: Compare again the 5 sunny days and the 3 rainy days.
z-m-04-07.s.s2.o.d: We collected ten days, so next week there will be exactly 3 sunny days
z-m-04-07.s.s2.r.d: You carried the ratio of the past records straight over to next week. Even if the records grow, you cannot decide the exact number of days for next week.
z-m-04-07.s.s3.prompt: Write what you can say about next week's weather from the data you have now, and what is still not certain. Also write what other records would make you trust that statement more.

z-m-04-08.title: The same buttons, but the most common one is different
z-m-04-08.topic: The 'most' changes depending on the standard: color, shape, kind
z-m-04-08.goal: Learn that when you sort the same buttons by color, by shape, or by kind counting color and shape together, the 'most' can be different, then choose the standard that fits the question and make a new question.
z-m-04-08.material: There are 12 buttons in a button shop. Each button is one of the colors red, blue, or yellow, and has a circle or triangle shape. [Table] Red circle 2 / Red triangle 3 / Blue circle 4 / Blue triangle 0 / Yellow circle 1 / Yellow triangle 2. Together they make 12. Minjun counted by color and also counted by shape.
z-m-04-08.thinking.0: Sorting the same data by several standards and comparing
z-m-04-08.thinking.1: Telling apart what each standard tells you and what it does not
z-m-04-08.thinking.2: Choosing the standard that fits the question
z-m-04-08.prereq.1: Sorting objects by color and shape
z-m-04-08.s.s1.prompt: This is how Minjun thought. Choose the wrong line.
z-m-04-08.s.s1.hint.0: Find and read the number in the 'red circle' box of the table.
z-m-04-08.s.s1.hint.1: Compare which of the six boxes has the biggest number.
z-m-04-08.s.s1.line.0: I counted by color: red 5, blue 4, yellow 3. The color with the most is red.
z-m-04-08.s.s1.line.1: I counted by shape: circle 7, triangle 5. The shape with the most is circle.
z-m-04-08.s.s1.line.2: So 'red circle' is the button there are the most of.
z-m-04-08.s.s1.line.3: Whether you count by color or by shape, it is 12 in all.
z-m-04-08.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. In the table there are only 2 red circles. Putting together the color with the most (red) and the shape with the most (circle) does not make the kind of button there are the most of. If you count the kind where both color and shape are the same, blue circle is the most with 4. Lines 1 and 2 match the table, and line 4 is right too.
z-m-04-08.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the statements that match what the button shop owner wants to do with the right table.
z-m-04-08.s.s2.hint.0: First say whether the question asks about color, about shape, or about both.
z-m-04-08.s.s2.hint.1: Find, one by one, which table shows the numbers the question needs.
z-m-04-08.s.s2.o.a: To decide 'Which shape of box should we buy more of?', you can look at the table sorted by color
z-m-04-08.s.s2.r.a: The table counted by color does not show the numbers for each shape. Match what the question asks with what the table tells you.
z-m-04-08.s.s2.o.b: To decide 'Which color of thread should we buy more of?', you can look at the table sorted by color
z-m-04-08.s.s2.r.b: The question asks about color, so you chose the table counted by color.
z-m-04-08.s.s2.o.c: For any question, one table sorted by color is enough
z-m-04-08.s.s2.r.c: You thought one table can answer every question. Different questions may need different tables.
z-m-04-08.s.s2.o.d: If you put together the color with the most and the shape with the most, you get the kind with the most
z-m-04-08.s.s2.r.d: Check again in the boxes of the table whether putting together the most in color and the most in shape works.
z-m-04-08.s.s2.o.e: 'Which button should we fill up first?' needs you to look at all six boxes
z-m-04-08.s.s2.r.e: You thought a question that looks at color and shape together needs a table that counts both color and shape.
z-m-04-08.s.s2.explain: For a question about color, the table counted by color fits; for a question about shape, the table counted by shape fits; and for a question about color and shape together, the table that looks at all six boxes fits. One table cannot answer every question.
z-m-04-08.s.s3.prompt: Make up another question the button shop owner could ask. Also write which table fits that question, the one counted by color, by shape, or by color and shape together, and why.
z-m-04-08.s.s3.hint.0: Imagine what the button shop owner wants to buy.
z-m-04-08.s.s3.hint.1: Try the table counted by color, the table counted by shape, and the six-box table against the question one by one and see whether an answer comes out.
z-m-04-08.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Which ... should we buy more of? ...
z-m-04-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you decide on the table that fits the question I made?
z-m-04-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write why the table I chose fits this question better than the other tables?
z-m-04-08.s.s3.model.0: 'Which shape of box should we buy more of?' For this question, you can look at the table sorted by shape. Because it tells you circle 7 and triangle 5.
z-m-04-08.s.s3.model.1: Which kind of button should we fill up first? The table counted by color and shape together fits. Because it tells you that blue circle is the most with 4.
z-m-04-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: Chose the table counted by color and shape together
